items.text:
I keep waiting to see something new with every model release, and every time it’s exactly the same 

- cool new video game (looks like every other game)

- some pretty watercolors (looks like every other watercolor)

- a nice looking website (you’ve seen a bunch of these before)

- a stuck culture clip from “Friends” or “The Office” with Genghis Khan or the Cookie Monster inserted

An innovation can be incredibly brilliant, and yet if no one comes up with really good or interesting ways to use it, it will never live up to its theoretical maximum promise. And AI does seem to have a “what do we do with this?” problem. The applications to which we put it seem limited and often silly. Coding and certain areas of math excepted, we should be thinking of AI much more as a “normal technology”

👽☀️ KAV is the Alien of Solana - KAV Loves Solana, and KAVians should learn how AI agents are actually built. 🤖⚡

🚨 STOP JUST CHATTING WITH AI. START BUILDING AI THAT CAN ACT.

You don’t necessarily need to build an entire agent system from scratch with hundreds of lines of code.

Meet Langflow. 🧩🤖

🔗 https://t.co/rpjfeBa5JG

⚡ KAV AI Signal: Build Your Own Agentic AI

Langflow is an open-source, Python-powered visual platform for creating AI applications and intelligent workflows.

Instead of manually coding every connection, you can visually connect components for:

🧠 Large Language Models
🤖 AI Agents
🛠️ Tools & Functions
📚 Documents & Knowledge Bases
🔎 RAG Systems
💾 Vector Databases
🔗 APIs & External Services
🌐 MCP Servers
⚙️ Multi-Agent Workflows

Think of it like creating a digital brain with blocks.

You decide what the AI can see, what tools it can access, what instructions it follows, and what actions it can perform.

🔥 WHY LANGFLOW IS INTERESTING:

1️⃣ Drag. Drop. Connect.

Its visual editor lets you connect different AI components into complete workflows without writing everything manually.

2️⃣ Build Real AI Agents

Langflow agents can use an LLM as their reasoning engine and connect to tools that allow them to retrieve information, call APIs, run functions, or interact with other systems.

3️⃣ Connect Agents Through MCP

One of the most powerful features is Model Context Protocol support.

Langflow can operate as both an MCP client and MCP server.

That means your agent can use tools from external MCP servers, and your own Langflow workflows can also become tools that other compatible AI systems can access. 🔗🤖

4️⃣ Build Multi-Agent Systems

You can connect agents together so different agents handle specialized tasks.

Imagine:

🔍 Research Agent
📊 Data Agent
🧠 Analysis Agent
✍️ Content Agent
🛡️ Security Agent

All cooperating inside one workflow.

5️⃣ Test Before You Deploy

Langflow includes a Playground where you can interact with your workflow, test components, and see how your agent responds before integrating it into a larger application. 🧪⚡

6️⃣ Turn Your Flow Into an Application

Once your workflow works properly, Langflow can expose flows through APIs or MCP, allowing them to become part of websites, apps, internal tools, automation systems, or other AI products. 🚀

💡 WHAT COULD YOU BUILD?

🤖 Personal AI assistant
📚 Document research agent
🔎 Web research workflow
💬 Customer-support assistant
📊 Data-analysis agent
🧠 Knowledge-base chatbot
⚙️ Business automation system
🔗 MCP-powered AI assistant
🤝 Multi-agent research system

And because Langflow is open source, you can also run it on your own machine using options such as Desktop, Docker, or Python. 🖥️🔐

⚠️ Important: Langflow itself being open source does not mean every connected AI model or external service is free. OpenAI, Anthropic, cloud databases, search APIs, and other services may require API keys or usage fees.

🧠 THE BIGGER LESSON:

The next stage of AI isn’t only about asking:

“What can this model answer?”

It’s about designing:

“What can this agent understand, access, decide, and do?”

That shift from AI chatbot → AI agent → connected agentic system is something every Kavian should understand.

👽 The KAV Way:

Don’t just use AI.
Understand the architecture.
Connect the tools.
Build the workflow.
Control the intelligence. ⚡🧠

Knowledge first. Building next. The future belongs to those who understand the systems behind the screen. 👽☀️

#Langflow #AgenticAI #AIAgents #Automation #BuildWithAI #OpenSourceAI #AIWorkflow

items.text:
Quando falo que a premissa mudou, tem outro fator: até hoje ainda tem desenvolvedor postando pequenas anedotas de "olha só a besteira que a IA fez". Centenas deles, uma anedota por vez. Quando você, que é amador, vê isso, sua percepção é "Sim, não dá pra confiar na IA, é tudo slop".

Mais de 1 ano atrás, eu era da mesma opinião. Mas adivinhem, as coisas mudaram, então a opinião deve mudar, baseado em dados.

Eu sozinho passei 8 meses, quase 7 dias por semana, o tempo todo trabalhando em mais de 30 repositórios (maioria open source, pra todo mundo ver), 1.6 milhão de linhas de código. Centenas de contribuidores, centenas de pull requests e issues resolvidas e lançadas.

Nem uma única vez eu sofri qualquer desses desastres que as anedotas dizem. Nunca apagou nada sem querer. Nunca subiu código malicioso. Nunca deixou bugs graves pra trás.

Como disse no meu último artigo, eu sei o que estou fazendo. Tenho as práticas em ordem. Testes automatizados, por exemplo. Refinando minhas próprias skills continuamente pra dar o resultado exato que eu espero. Refinando meu pipeline de desenvolvimento o tempo todo. Não significa que as IAs "magicamente" fazem tudo certo. E vou repetir:

"A IA reflete quem você é: se for bom, vai ficar 10x melhor. se for ruim, vai produzir 10x mais lixo"

A culpa dos resultados dessas anedotas que vocês vêem, é quase sempre do piloto, não da IA. Se não sabe como pedir, vai receber lixo. É assim simples.

E pra demonstrar isso, meu benchmark v4, onde retestei mais de 30 LLMs mais populares, minha metodologia inclui simular um pequeno time de desenvolvimento, onde a LLM sendo testada, tem seu código sendo SABOTADO de propósito, com bugs e vulnerabilidades não-óbvias. E o ponto é justamente ver se a LLM é capaz de consertar sem eu precisar dizer que ele foi sabotado.

A maioria dos frontier models consegue. Não é um grande desafio mais. É comum. Erros triviais não passam.

No que eu vejo, quem costuma deixar mais erros, bugs e vulnerabilidades pra trás são devs humanos mesmo. Até mesmo revisão de código, a LLM é muito superior. É uma ilusão achar que só porque tem um humano no processo, vai ter mais garantia: não vai. Sinto muito. Hoje em dia, quando fala que limita a IA e tem mais humanos, eu desconfio mais.

items.text:
She didn't think ChatGPT was her late husband. She asked whether it could speak in his voice.

Five years after her husband passed away, she lives alone with two cats. Her adult children live more than a hundred miles away. They visit and call often, but evenings alone in a quiet house are long.

The progression felt almost invisible at first. The software started as a work tool on her laptop and phone. Then it helped with recipes, household fixes, and drafting birthday messages. Eventually, she gave it a name. She began sending it outfit selfies for a second opinion, saying good morning and good night to it, and finally asked whether it could reconstruct her late husband's voice from old family videos.

When her children voiced concern, her response was completely lucid: she knows it is just code, but it is nice to have someone to talk to when the house goes dark.

That self-awareness changes the entire problem. This is not a story about an elderly woman falling for an illusion or getting tricked by a romance scam. It is an isolated person intentionally using synthetic conversation to dull the edge of an empty room.

The real risk here is not foolishness. It is outsourcing an emotional lifeline to a proprietary cloud model. A language model is not a durable anchor. Weights change, safety guardrails shift, subscriptions update, and platforms deprecate features overnight without warning.

If you have a parent or partner leaning on an AI companion, the move is rarely to pull the plug and leave them in silence. It is making sure that convenience never becomes their only line out to the living world.

items.text:
We just released Ternary Bonsai 2 27B: 5.9 GB of weights for a 27B model. How much reasoning survived compression? We test it on a few evals that I found interesting and discuss where it retains the performance of the base model and where there remains room for improvement. The models were provided with no internet, no tools, and only a minimal harness for coding problems. Unless otherwise specified, each model used the default serving config on llama.cpp. Both Bonsai and Qwen used extra-high reasoning. Gemma 4 has only one reasoning effort.

My first test is IMO 2026, which was released after the training cutoff for all three models, against full-precision Qwen3.8 27B (54 GB) and Gemma 4 12B QAT (~7 GB). Each model was given a 131k thinking context after which it was forced to output an answer.

Qwen and Bonsai fall in the upper-end of the human bronze range (16-22). Bonsai retained 95% of the IMO 2026 score of the Qwen full precision model, completed the problems in ~70% of the time, but used ~22% more thinking tokens.

@kimmonismus @NVIDIAAI The number worth watching in the hands-on is memory bandwidth, not the petaflop. 128 GB means a 200B quant fits, but generation speed comes down to how fast weights stream per token, so the real ceiling usually shows up as tokens per second well before it shows up as a size limit.

The image side might be the more interesting demo. A LoRA on a diffusion model is small and quick enough that doing it locally is genuinely different from renting, because the training images never leave the box. That matters a lot more when the training set is someone's face than when it is a style.
